lines.text: This is a seal. In Japan, it's called a hanko. You stamp it to say: I approve.
Its first character also means judgment.
And that's the point. A seal is only worth the judgment behind it. Years of practice. An eye that sees what's wrong.
Now picture a print workshop. A master. Her apprentices.
Every print passes under her eye before it gets her seal.
Then the paper cranes arrive. They're AI agents: programs that do the work on their own. They never sleep.
At Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, agents now work six hours for every human hour.
But mostly, they wait. Eighty percent of the time, they're waiting for a human to check their work.
So someone puts an abacus on the desk. A dashboard.
It counts, and makes experts and juniors alike look like they're just waiting.
And waiting is a cost.
Looking became waiting. Waiting became a cost.
So the workshop stops taking apprentices. At Anthropic, juniors fell from twenty-seven percent of technical hires to nine. In one year.
No apprentices today. No masters tomorrow. No judgment the day after that.
That part is already very real. In software, for instance, experienced engineers are kept, because software is hard to maintain.
Juniors are harder to justify. And the experienced will retire, someday soon.
With less judgment around, checking looks even less necessary. So it ends up being cut again.
This happens time and time again. Firms bet on machines that aren't ready yet, and the bet makes itself come true.
If they're wrong, someone else pays: the junior who was never hired.
Bet on the machine. If you're wrong, someone else pays.
I wanted to see where this loop ends. So I built a model: a small simulated world, with explicit rules.
You turn the dials. It plays the loop forward five hundred times, to 2060.
And it measures one thing: how much real judgment still stands behind each seal.
In most futures, the seal survives. The judgment behind it drains away.
The seal remains. The judgment is gone.
Europe was the surprise. Its AI law requires a human to oversee risky AI. A human seal. In my model, that helps. Europe keeps more judgment than America.
But it protects the seal, perhaps more than necessary. So, in ninety-four European futures out of a hundred, the seal outlives the judgment behind it. In America, only forty-four.
In Europe, the law guarantees the seal. Unfortunately, not the judgment behind it.
My model is completely unfinished. It misses several checks against real data, and it doesn't have enough of that exquisite data yet.
Part of the Europe result comes from my own assumptions, and from what I've read.
It forgets the hidden workers who train the machines. And India. And the Global South.
And nobody publishes the number that my model needs the most to be accurate: how often a human seal actually changes what a machine proposed.

So why does this all matter? Why does it need fixing? Because a model like this, made right, could be used before the cuts, not after. A company could see what judgment it will still have in ten years, before it stops hiring juniors.
A regulator could test whether a rule protects people's judgment, or only their signatures.
So everything is open: the model, the code, the sources, the mistakes.
Take a brush. Help me fix it. It's yours.
Help me fix it.
